title: An Exact and Sustainable Analysis of Non-preemptive Scheduling

extraction.paper_name: An Exact and Sustainable Analysis of Non-Preemptive Scheduling
extraction.paper_description: This paper presents an exact and sustainable schedulability test for non-preemptive fixed-job-priority (FJP) scheduling on a uniprocessor, supporting both work-conserving and non-work-conserving schedulers with release jitter and execution time variation. It constructs a schedule graph with a novel path-merging technique to abstract all possible execution scenarios and derive tight best- and worst-case response time bounds.

formal_description.statement: An execution scenario `gamma = (C, R)` for a set of jobs `job_set` is a sequence of execution times `C = C_1, C_2, ..., C_m` and release times `R = r_1, r_2, ..., r_m` such that, for each job `job_i`, `C_i` is in `[C_min_i, C_max_i]` and `r_i` is in `[r_min_i, r_max_i]`.

variables.C: sequence of actual execution times for jobs
variables.R: sequence of actual release times for jobs
variables.job_set: the finite set of all jobs being scheduled
variables.C_i: actual execution time of job_i in this scenario
variables.r_i: actual release time of job_i in this scenario
variables.r_min_i: earliest release time of job_i (expected release time minus jitter)
variables.r_max_i: latest release time of job_i (expected release time plus jitter)

assumptions: job_set is a finite set of non-preemptive jobs
Execution times and release times are bounded by min/max values
formal_description.conclusion: Defines what constitutes a valid 'execution scenario' for a given set of jobs, capturing variations in execution and release times.

informal_sketch.intuition: An execution scenario describes one specific way the jobs in the system could behave. It specifies the exact execution time and release time for each job, within their allowed ranges. The system must be schedulable for ALL such scenarios.
steps: For each job `job_i` in the `job_set`:
Assign an actual execution time `C_i` such that `C_min_i <= C_i <= C_max_i`.
Assign an actual release time `r_i` such that `r_min_i <= r_i <= r_max_i`.
The collection of these `C_i` and `r_i` values forms one `gamma`.
key_insights: Captures the inherent uncertainty (release jitter, execution time variation) in real-time systems.
Schedulability analysis must account for all possible scenarios, not just a single 'worst-case' one.

formal_description.statement: A possibly released job `job_j` is priority-eligible at time `t` iff `job_j` is in `job_set \ jobs_in_path_P` such that `r_min_j <= t` AND there is no `job_x` in `job_set \ jobs_in_path_P` such that `r_max_x <= t` AND `p_x < p_j`.

variables.job_j: the job being checked for priority eligibility
variables.job_set: the finite set of all jobs
variables.jobs_in_path_P: the set of jobs already scheduled in the current path `P`
variables.p_x: priority of job_x (lower value means higher priority)

assumptions: Priorities are fixed (FJP policy)
Tie-breaking rules are implicit in the '<' priority order.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines when a job `job_j` *could* be the highest-priority pending job at time `t`, considering only priority and release times.

informal_sketch.intuition: A job is priority-eligible if it's potentially ready to run (its earliest release time is by `t`) AND no other job that is *certainly* ready by `t` has a higher priority.
steps: Check if `job_j` has already been scheduled in the current path. If so, it's not eligible.
Check if `job_j` could possibly be released by `t` (`r_min_j <= t`). If not, it's not eligible.
Iterate through all other pending jobs `job_x` (not in `jobs_in_path_P` and not `job_j`):
If `job_x` is *certainly* released by `t` (`r_max_x <= t`) AND `job_x` has higher priority than `job_j` (`p_x < p_j`), then `job_j` is NOT priority-eligible.
If no such `job_x` is found, `job_j` IS priority-eligible.
key_insights: Uses `r_min_j` for `job_j` (optimistic for `job_j`'s release) and `r_max_x` for `job_x` (pessimistic for `job_x`'s release) to determine if `job_j` *could* be the highest priority.
Filters out jobs that are definitely blocked by higher-priority jobs.

formal_description.statement: A job `job_j` is IIP-eligible at time `t` iff the IIP permits it to be scheduled, i.e., iff `t <= L_job_j_t_jobs_in_path_P`.

variables.job_j: the job being checked for IIP eligibility
variables.L_job_j_t_jobs_in_path_P: the latest permissible start time for job_j at time t, given the set of completed jobs `jobs_in_path_P` (determined by the Idle-Time Insertion Policy)
variables.jobs_in_path_P: the set of jobs already scheduled in the current path `P`

assumptions: The JIIP function `L_job_j_t_jobs_in_path_P` is defined and stable (i.e., once it blocks a job, it continues to block it until the set of scheduled jobs changes).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines when a job `job_j` is allowed to be scheduled by the Idle-Time Insertion Policy (IIP) at time `t`.

informal_sketch.intuition: Even if a job is the highest priority, a non-work-conserving scheduler might decide to idle the processor. This definition checks if the IIP allows the job to run at the given time `t`.
steps: Call the IIP function `L` with `job_j`, `t`, and `jobs_in_path_P` to get the latest permissible start time.
If `t` is less than or equal to this latest permissible start time, then `job_j` is IIP-eligible.
key_insights: Integrates non-work-conserving scheduling policies into the analysis.
The `L` function is crucial for determining if idle time is inserted.

formal_description.statement:
A job `job_j` is potentially next at time `t` iff either:
(i) `job_j` can be released before `l_i`, i.e., `r_min_j <= l_i`, OR
(ii) no other job `job_x` in `job_set \ jobs_in_path_P` (where `job_x` is not `job_j` and `r_max_x < t`) is both priority-eligible and IIP-eligible at time `max(r_max_x, l_i)`.

variables.job_j: the job being checked for potential next eligibility
variables.l_i: the latest finish time (LFT) of the last job in the current path `P` (ending at `vertex_v_i`)
variables.job_set: the finite set of all jobs
variables.jobs_in_path_P: the set of jobs already scheduled in the current path `P`

assumptions: The scheduler is eager (does not leave the processor idle if a job is allowed to run).
Definitions 2 and 3 for priority-eligible and IIP-eligible are available.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines when a job `job_j` can logically be the *immediate* successor to the current path, considering its release time relative to the current path's finish time and the absence of other jobs that *must* run before it.

informal_sketch.intuition: A job can be scheduled next if it's either ready by the time the previous job finishes (even its latest finish time), OR if the processor would definitely be idle until `job_j`'s earliest start time because no other job is certainly ready and allowed to run.
steps: Check Clause (i): If `job_j.r_min <= l_i`, then `job_j` is potentially next.
If Clause (i) is false, check Clause (ii):
Iterate through all other pending jobs `job_x` (not in `jobs_in_path_P` and not `job_j`):
If `job_x` is *certainly* released before `t` (`r_max_x < t`):
Determine `check_time = max(job_x.r_max, l_i)`.
If `job_x` is both `is_priority_eligible(job_x, check_time, ...)` AND `is_iip_eligible(job_x, check_time, ...)`, then `job_j` is NOT potentially next (because `job_x` would run first).
If no such `job_x` is found, `job_j` IS potentially next.
key_insights: Crucial for correctly modeling idle times inserted by non-work-conserving schedulers.
Ensures that if `job_j` is chosen, no other job *must* have run before it, even if the processor idles.

formal_description.statement: A job `job_j` in `job_set \ jobs_in_path_P` is an eligible successor for path `path_P` ending in vertex `vertex_v_i` iff `job_j` is IIP-eligible, priority-eligible, and potentially next at time `t_E = max(vertex_v_i.eft, r_min_j)`.

variables.job_j: the job being checked for eligible successor status
variables.job_set: the finite set of all jobs
variables.jobs_in_path_P: the set of jobs already scheduled in the current path `path_P`
variables.path_P: the current path in the schedule graph
variables.vertex_v_i.eft: the earliest finish time (EFT) of the job sequence ending at `vertex_v_i`

assumptions: Definitions 2, 3, and 4 are available.
The scheduler is FJP, uses a stable JIIP (or no IIP), and is eager.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the complete set of conditions for a job to be considered as the *next* job in a schedule sequence, used for expanding the schedule graph.

informal_sketch.intuition: This combines all the previous eligibility checks. A job can be the next one in the schedule if, at its earliest possible start time, it's the highest priority, the IIP allows it, and no other job *must* run before it.
steps: Calculate `t_E = max(vertex_v_i.eft, job_j.r_min)`.
Check if `job_j` is `is_iip_eligible` at `t_E`.
Check if `job_j` is `is_priority_eligible` at `t_E`.
Check if `job_j` is `is_potentially_next` at `t_E` (using `vertex_v_i.lft` for `l_i`).
If all three conditions are true, `job_j` is an eligible successor.
key_insights: This definition is the core filtering mechanism for determining which jobs can extend a given path in the schedule graph.
It ensures that the graph only explores valid and relevant sequences of jobs.

formal_description.statement: A path `path_Q` from `v_1` to `vertex_v_q` is matching a given path `path_P` from `v_1` to `vertex_v_p` iff `jobs_in_path_P = jobs_in_path_Q` AND the intersection of `[vertex_v_q.eft, vertex_v_q.lft]` and `[vertex_v_p.eft, vertex_v_p.lft]` is not empty.

variables.v_1: the root vertex of the schedule graph
variables.jobs_in_path_P: the set of jobs (edge labels) in `path_P`
variables.jobs_in_path_Q: the set of jobs (edge labels) in `path_Q`
variables.vertex_v_q.eft: earliest finish time of the sequence ending at `vertex_v_q`
variables.vertex_v_q.lft: latest finish time of the sequence ending at `vertex_v_q`
variables.vertex_v_p.eft: earliest finish time of the sequence ending at `vertex_v_p`
variables.vertex_v_p.lft: latest finish time of the sequence ending at `vertex_v_p`

assumptions: Paths are sequences of jobs from the root.
Vertex labels `[eft, lft]` represent the finish time interval of the sequence.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines when two paths in the schedule graph are considered 'similar enough' to be merged, which is a key step for graph compaction.

informal_sketch.intuition: Two paths are considered 'matching' if they have scheduled the exact same set of jobs (regardless of order) AND their possible finish time intervals overlap. If they overlap, it means there's at least one scenario where both paths could lead to a similar final state, so they can be merged.
steps: Extract the set of job IDs from `path_P` and `path_Q`.
If these sets are not identical, the paths do not match.
Get the `[eft, lft]` intervals for `vertex_v_p` and `vertex_v_q`.
Check if `max(vertex_v_q.eft, vertex_v_p.eft) <= min(vertex_v_q.lft, vertex_v_p.lft)`. If true, the intervals overlap, and the paths match.
key_insights: This is the core of the path-merging technique, essential for controlling state-space explosion.
Merging paths with overlapping finish time intervals preserves analysis precision while reducing graph size.

results.identifier: Formula for Earliest Finish Time (EFT) of a new vertex

variables.e_k: the earliest finish time (EFT) of the new vertex `vertex_v_k` (representing `job_j`'s completion)
variables.t_E: the earliest start time of `job_j` (calculated as `max(vertex_v_i.eft, r_min_j)`)

assumptions: The previous job in the path finishes at `vertex_v_i.eft`.
`job_j` is released at `r_min_j`.
`job_j` executes for its minimum time `C_min_j`.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the earliest possible time `job_j` can finish if it is scheduled next.

informal_sketch.intuition: The fastest a job can finish is by starting as early as possible and executing for its minimum duration.
steps: Determine `t_E`, the earliest `job_j` can start (which is the later of when the previous job finishes and when `job_j` is earliest released).
Add `job_j`'s best-case execution time (`C_min_j`) to `t_E`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_eft_for_next_job(prev_vertex_eft, job_j_r_min, job_j_c_min):
    t_E = max(prev_vertex_eft, job_j_r_min)
    e_k = t_E + job_j_c_min
    return e_k
key_insights: Combines the earliest possible start time with the minimum execution time to find the absolute earliest completion.

results.identifier: Formula for Latest Start Time Component t_L

variables.t_L: a component of the latest start time for `job_j`
variables.l_i: the latest finish time (LFT) of the last job in the current path `P` (ending at `vertex_v_i`)

assumptions: The previous job in the path finishes at `l_i`.
`job_j` is certainly released by `r_max_j`.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a bound on `job_j`'s latest start time based on when the previous job certainly finishes and when `job_j` is certainly released.

informal_sketch.intuition: A job cannot start until the processor is free (previous job finished) AND it is certainly released. So, its start time is bounded by the later of these two events.
steps: Take the latest finish time of the preceding job (`l_i`).
Take the latest release time of `job_j` (`r_max_j`).
The maximum of these two values is `t_L`.
key_insights: Ensures that `job_j` is not considered to start before all preceding conditions are met in the worst case.

results.identifier: Formula for Latest Start Time Component t_H

formal_description.statement: `t_H = infinity`, if `higher_priority_pending_jobs` is empty; `min(r_max_x for job_x in higher_priority_pending_jobs) - 1` otherwise.

variables.t_H: a component of the latest start time for `job_j`
variables.higher_priority_pending_jobs: the set of jobs `job_x` such that `job_x` is in `job_set \ jobs_in_path_P` and `p_x < p_j` (i.e., incomplete higher-priority jobs)
variables.jobs_in_path_P: the set of jobs already scheduled in the current path `P`

assumptions: The scheduler is Fixed-Job-Priority (FJP).
A job cannot commence execution if a higher-priority job is certainly released.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a bound on `job_j`'s latest start time based on when a higher-priority job is certainly released.

informal_sketch.intuition: A job must start before any higher-priority job is *certainly* released, because once a higher-priority job is certainly released, `job_j` can no longer be the highest-priority pending job and thus cannot start.
steps: Identify all jobs `job_x` that are not yet scheduled and have higher priority than `job_j`.
If there are no such jobs, `t_H` is infinite (no higher-priority constraint).
Otherwise, find the minimum `r_max_x` among these higher-priority jobs.
Subtract 1 from this minimum `r_max_x` to get `t_H` (as `job_j` must start *before* this time).
key_insights: Captures the blocking effect of higher-priority jobs in a non-preemptive FJP scheduler.
Uses `r_max_x` to ensure the 'certainly released' condition for higher-priority jobs.

results.identifier: Formula for Latest Finish Time (LFT) of a new vertex

variables.l_k: the latest finish time (LFT) of the new vertex `vertex_v_k` (representing `job_j`'s completion)
variables.t_L: latest start time component considering previous job finish and `job_j`'s release
variables.t_H: latest start time component considering higher-priority jobs
variables.t_I: latest start time component considering the IIP (i.e., `L_job_j_t_E_jobs_in_path_P`)

assumptions: The scheduler is FJP, uses a stable JIIP (or no IIP), and is eager.
`job_j` executes for its maximum time `C_max_j`.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the latest possible time `job_j` can finish if it is scheduled next.

informal_sketch.intuition: The latest a job can finish is by starting as late as possible (constrained by all factors) and executing for its maximum duration.
steps: Calculate `t_L` (max of previous job's LFT and `job_j`'s `r_max`).
Calculate `t_H` (min `r_max` of higher-priority jobs minus 1, or infinity).
Calculate `t_I` (the IIP's latest permissible start time for `job_j` at `t_E`).
The latest `job_j` can start is the minimum of `t_L`, `t_H`, and `t_I`.
Add `job_j`'s worst-case execution time (`C_max_j`) to this latest start time.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_lft_for_next_job(prev_vertex_lft, job_j, jobs_in_path_P, all_jobs, iip_function_L, t_E):
    t_L = calculate_t_L(prev_vertex_lft, job_j.r_max)
    t_H = calculate_t_H(job_j, jobs_in_path_P, all_jobs)
    t_I = iip_function_L(job_j, t_E, jobs_in_path_P) # t_E is max(prev_vertex_eft, job_j.r_min)
    
    latest_start_time = min(t_L, t_H, t_I)
    l_k = latest_start_time + job_j.c_max
    return l_k
key_insights: Combines all worst-case factors (previous job finish, higher-priority interference, IIP blocking) with maximum execution time to find the absolute latest completion.

dependencies: Formula for Latest Start Time Component t_L
Formula for Latest Start Time Component t_H

variables.vertex_v_q: the source vertex being merged into `vertex_v_p`

assumptions: The two vertices `vertex_v_p` and `vertex_v_q` represent matching paths (Definition 6).
formal_description.conclusion: Describes how the finish time interval of a vertex is updated when another path's ending vertex is merged into it, ensuring the combined interval covers all possibilities from both paths.

informal_sketch.intuition: When two paths are merged, the resulting vertex must represent all possible finish times from both original paths. This means its EFT becomes the minimum of the two original EFTs, and its LFT becomes the maximum of the two original LFTs.
steps: Update `vertex_v_p.eft = min(vertex_v_p.eft, vertex_v_q.eft)`.
Update `vertex_v_p.lft = max(vertex_v_p.lft, vertex_v_q.lft)`.
key_insights: This operation is crucial for maintaining the 'exactness' of the analysis during the graph merging phase.
It ensures that no possible finish times are lost when paths are collapsed.

formal_description.statement: The EFT (`e_p`) and LFT (`l_p`) of a newly created vertex `vertex_v_p` cannot be smaller than `e_k` (from Formula for Earliest Finish Time) or larger than `l_k` (from Formula for Latest Finish Time), respectively.

variables.e_p: the earliest finish time of the new vertex `vertex_v_p`
variables.l_p: the latest finish time of the new vertex `vertex_v_p`
variables.l_k: the calculated LFT using `min(t_L, t_H, t_I) + C_max_j`

assumptions: The inductive hypothesis holds: previous vertex labels are exact bounds.
The formulas for `e_k` and `l_k` are correctly applied.
formal_description.conclusion: Equations (3) and (5) (for `e_k` and `l_k`) provide tight lower and upper bounds for the finish times of a job `job_j` when it is scheduled next.

informal_sketch.intuition: The formulas used to calculate the earliest and latest finish times are accurate. You cannot finish earlier than the calculated EFT, and you cannot finish later than the calculated LFT, given the system model and scheduler behavior.
steps: Base case: The root vertex has EFT=0, LFT=0, which is trivially tight.
Inductive step: Assume the EFT/LFT of the previous vertex `vertex_v_i` are tight.
For EFT: `job_j` cannot start before `max(vertex_v_i.eft, job_j.r_min)` and cannot execute faster than `job_j.c_min`. Thus, `e_k` is a tight lower bound.
For LFT: `job_j` must start by `min(t_L, t_H, t_I)` and cannot execute slower than `job_j.c_max`. Thus, `l_k` is a tight upper bound.

# It asserts that the calculated EFT and LFT values are indeed the tightest possible bounds.
# No direct pseudocode for this lemma, as it validates the formulas themselves.
key_insights: Establishes the fundamental correctness of the EFT/LFT calculations, which are central to the schedulability analysis.
Guarantees that the bounds derived are not overly pessimistic or optimistic.

Formula for Latest Finish Time (LFT) of a new vertex

formal_description.statement: For every vertex `vertex_v_p` in `V` and any time `t` in `[vertex_v_p.eft, vertex_v_p.lft]`, there exists an execution scenario and a corresponding path `path_P = v_1, ..., vertex_v_p` such that the last job in the job sequence represented by `path_P` finishes by time `t`.

variables.vertex_v_p: a vertex in the schedule graph
variables.V: the set of all vertices in the schedule graph
variables.vertex_v_p.eft: earliest finish time of the sequence ending at `vertex_v_p`
variables.vertex_v_p.lft: latest finish time of the sequence ending at `vertex_v_p`
variables.path_P: a path from the root `v_1` to `vertex_v_p`

assumptions: The schedule graph is constructed by Algorithm 2.
The inductive hypothesis holds: for the preceding vertex `vertex_v_i`, any time in `[vertex_v_i.eft, vertex_v_i.lft]` is reachable.
formal_description.conclusion: Every time point within the `[eft, lft]` interval of a vertex `vertex_v_p` is reachable by some execution scenario, meaning the interval is continuous and fully covered.

informal_sketch.intuition: The finish time interval `[eft, lft]` for any vertex is not just a bound, but it accurately represents a continuous range of possible finish times. There are no 'gaps' in the possible finish times that the graph fails to capture.
steps: Base case: The root vertex `v_1` has `[0,0]`, which is trivially covered.
Inductive step: Assume the claim holds for `vertex_v_i` (the predecessor of `vertex_v_p`).

For any `t` in `[vertex_v_p.eft, vertex_v_p.lft]`, construct an execution scenario (by carefully choosing `C_j` and `r_j` for `job_j` and its predecessors) that results in `job_j` finishing exactly at `t`.
This involves considering four cases based on the relative values of `e_i`, `l_i`, `r_min_j`, `r_max_j`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
# This lemma is a proof statement about the completeness of the vertex intervals.
# It asserts that for any time 't' within a vertex's [eft, lft] interval,
# a valid execution scenario can be constructed to achieve that finish time.
# No direct pseudocode for this lemma, as it validates the interval coverage.
key_insights: Guarantees the 'exactness' of the analysis by ensuring that the schedule graph does not miss any possible finish times.
Crucial for deriving tight best- and worst-case response times.

Formula for Latest Finish Time (LFT) of a new vertex

formal_description.statement: Job `job_j` is scheduled in some execution scenario as the next job in the job sequence represented by a path to a vertex `vertex_v_i` iff it is an eligible successor (Definition 5).

variables.vertex_v_i: the last vertex of the current path `P`
variables.path_P: the current path in the schedule graph

assumptions: The scheduler is FJP, uses a stable JIIP (or no IIP), and is eager.
Definitions 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correctly applied.
Lemma 2 holds (interval coverage).
formal_description.conclusion: Definition 5 provides a necessary and sufficient condition for a job to be scheduled next in some possible execution scenario.

informal_sketch.intuition: The `is_eligible_successor` function (based on Definition 5) perfectly identifies which jobs can run next. It doesn't miss any possibilities, and it doesn't include any impossibilities.
steps: Proof 'If' (sufficiency): If `job_j` is an eligible successor, construct an execution scenario (by setting `r_j = r_min_j`, other `r_x = r_max_x`, and choosing `C_x` values) that forces `job_j` to be scheduled next. Lemma 2 is used to ensure the predecessor can finish at the required time.

Proof 'Only if' (necessity): If `job_j` is NOT an eligible successor (i.e., it fails one of the conditions in Definition 5), show that no execution scenario can lead to `job_j` being scheduled next. This relies on the properties of FJP, stable IIP, and eager scheduling.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:

# It asserts that the function is both complete (finds all possible next jobs)
# and sound (does not find any impossible next jobs).
# No direct pseudocode for this lemma, as it validates the definition.
key_insights: Ensures the schedule graph accurately captures all possible job sequences without over- or under-approximation.
This is a critical step for the 'exactness' claim of the overall analysis.

formal_description.statement: If Algorithm 2 terminates successfully, then there exists an execution scenario such that a job `job_j` in `job_set` completes at some time `t` (under the given scheduler) iff there exists a path `path_P = v_1, ..., vertex_v_i, vertex_v_p` in the schedule graph such that `job_j` is the label of the edge from `vertex_v_i` to `vertex_v_p` and `t` is in `[e, l]`, where `e` and `l` are given by Formula for Earliest Finish Time and Formula for Latest Finish Time, respectively.

variables.job_set: the finite set of all jobs
variables.path_P: a path in the schedule graph
variables.vertex_v_i: a vertex in the path, preceding `vertex_v_p`

assumptions: Algorithm 2 (Schedule Graph Generation Algorithm) terminates successfully.
The scheduler is FJP, uses a stable JIIP (or no IIP), and is eager.
formal_description.conclusion: The schedule graph constructed by Algorithm 2 precisely abstracts all possible execution scenarios and their resulting job completion times, making the analysis exact.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the main correctness theorem. It states that the schedule graph is a perfect model of the system's behavior. Any job completion time that can occur in the real system is represented in the graph, and any completion time represented in the graph can occur in the real system.
steps: The theorem relies on the tightness of EFT/LFT bounds (Lemma 1), ensuring no impossible times are included.
It relies on the coverage of EFT/LFT intervals (Lemma 2), ensuring no possible times are missed.
It relies on the accuracy of eligible successor selection (Lemma 3), ensuring all valid job sequences are explored and no invalid ones are included.
Together, these lemmas guarantee that the graph is an 'exact abstraction' of all possible schedules.

It means that schedulability can be determined by simply inspecting the graph.

variables.BCRT_j: the best-case response time of job `job_j`
variables.e: the earliest finish time (EFT) of a vertex `vertex_v_p`
variables.vertex_v_p: a vertex in the schedule graph
variables.A_j: the set of vertices `vertex_v_p` such that `job_j` is the label of the incoming edge to `vertex_v_p` (i.e., `vertex_v_p` represents `job_j`'s completion)

assumptions: The schedule graph has been successfully generated by Algorithm 2.
The EFTs (`e`) of vertices are accurate (from Theorem 1).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the best-case response time of job `job_j` by finding its earliest possible completion time across all scenarios and subtracting its earliest release time.

informal_sketch.intuition: The best-case response time is the shortest possible time from a job's earliest release until its earliest completion. To find this, we look at all paths where `job_j` finishes and pick the one with the absolute earliest finish time.
steps: Identify all vertices `vertex_v_p` in the schedule graph where `job_j` is the last job scheduled to reach that vertex.
Find the minimum `e` (EFT) among all these `vertex_v_p`.
Subtract `job_j.r_min` from this minimum `e`.
key_insights: Provides a precise measure of the fastest a job can complete, useful for performance analysis or soft real-time guarantees.

formal_description.statement: `WCRT_j = max(l for vertex_v_p in A_j) - r_min_j`

variables.WCRT_j: the worst-case response time of job `job_j`
variables.l: the latest finish time (LFT) of a vertex `vertex_v_p`
variables.vertex_v_p: a vertex in the schedule graph
variables.A_j: the set of vertices `vertex_v_p` such that `job_j` is the label of the incoming edge to `vertex_v_p` (i.e., `vertex_v_p` represents `job_j`'s completion)

assumptions: The schedule graph has been successfully generated by Algorithm 2.
The LFTs (`l`) of vertices are accurate (from Theorem 1).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the worst-case response time of job `job_j` by finding its latest possible completion time across all scenarios and subtracting its earliest release time.

informal_sketch.intuition: The worst-case response time is the longest possible time from a job's earliest release until its latest completion. To find this, we look at all paths where `job_j` finishes and pick the one with the absolute latest finish time.
steps: Identify all vertices `vertex_v_p` in the schedule graph where `job_j` is the last job scheduled to reach that vertex.
Find the maximum `l` (LFT) among all these `vertex_v_p`.
Subtract `job_j.r_min` from this maximum `l`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_wcrt(job_j, schedule_graph):
    max_finish_time = 0
    # A_j is the set of vertices where job_j is the *last* job on the path
    for vertex_v_p in schedule_graph.get_completion_vertices_for_job(job_j):
        max_finish_time = max(max_finish_time, vertex_v_p.lft)
    
    # If max_finish_time is still 0 and job_j.r_min is 0, this might be okay.
    # A more robust check for non-completion might be needed if job_j is not found in A_j.
    return max_finish_time - job_j.r_min
key_insights: This is the primary metric for hard real-time schedulability analysis.
Its accuracy is guaranteed by the exactness of the schedule graph (Theorem 1).

formal_description.statement: A job set `job_set` is schedulable under a given scheduling policy if `WCRT_j <= job_j.relative_deadline` for every `job_j` in `job_set`.

variables.job_set: the finite set of all jobs
variables.WCRT_j: the worst-case response time of job `job_j`
variables.job_j.relative_deadline: the relative deadline of job `job_j` (which is `d_j - r_min_j` in the paper's notation)

assumptions: The system operates in a hard real-time context.
The `WCRT_j` for all jobs can be accurately determined (e.g., using the proposed analysis).
formal_description.conclusion: Provides the condition for a job set to be deemed schedulable, meaning all jobs meet their deadlines in all possible execution scenarios.

informal_sketch.intuition: For a system to be considered 'hard real-time schedulable', every single job must always complete its execution before its deadline, even in the absolute worst-case scenario. If any job's worst-case response time exceeds its deadline, the system is not schedulable.
steps: For each job `job_j` in the `job_set`:
Calculate its `WCRT_j`.
Compare `WCRT_j` with `job_j.relative_deadline`.
If `WCRT_j > job_j.relative_deadline` for any `job_j`, the `job_set` is NOT schedulable.
If all jobs satisfy `WCRT_j <= job_j.relative_deadline`, the `job_set` IS schedulable.
key_insights: This is the standard definition of hard real-time schedulability.
The challenge is to accurately compute `WCRT_j` for all jobs, which the paper's analysis aims to solve.

results.identifier: Necessary Schedulability Condition for Non-Preemptive Tasks

formal_description.statement: For a set of `n` non-preemptive tasks, a necessary schedulability condition is `C_max_i <= 2 * (T_1 - C_max_1)` for all `i` from `2` to `n`, where `T_1` is the shortest period and `C_max_1` is the WCET of the task with the shortest period.

variables.T_1: period of the task with the shortest period
variables.C_max_1: worst-case execution time of the task with the shortest period

assumptions: The tasks are periodic and non-preemptive.
Tasks are indexed such that task 1 has the shortest period.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a simple, necessary condition that must hold for a non-preemptive task set to be schedulable. If this condition is violated, the task set is guaranteed to be unschedulable.

informal_sketch.intuition: In non-preemptive scheduling, a lower-priority job can block a higher-priority job. This condition ensures that no job (except possibly the highest priority one) is so long that it would prevent the highest priority job from meeting its deadline, even if the highest priority job is released immediately after the current job starts.
steps: Identify the task with the shortest period (`T_1`) and its WCET (`C_max_1`).
For every other task `task_i` (i.e., `i` from 2 to `n`):
Check if `task_i.C_max` is greater than `2 * (T_1 - C_max_1)`.
If it is, the task set is unschedulable.
If all tasks satisfy the condition, the task set *might* be schedulable (further tests are needed).
key_insights: This is a quick, preliminary check for non-preemptive schedulability.
It highlights the critical impact of blocking from lower-priority jobs in non-preemptive systems.
